mcqs.question: A model performs well in offline evaluation but noticeably worse in production, with no errors or exceptions anywhere in the system. Training used a batch SQL pipeline to compute features; serving uses a separate low-latency service reimplementing the same feature logic. What is the most likely cause?
options: Training-serving skew — the two independently-implemented feature pipelines likely compute the "same" feature slightly differently, so the model sees systematically different inputs in production than it learned from
The model must be underfit, since offline and online performance should always match otherwise
This gap can only be caused by a labeling error in the training data
The production service must have a memory leak
mcqs.explanation: This is the textbook signature of training-serving skew: two separately maintained implementations of the same conceptual feature drift apart in some edge case (rounding, time windows, null handling), producing a silent, error-free accuracy gap between offline and online. Underfitting would typically show up in both offline and online results, not just online (A is false), a labeling error is one possible but not the most likely explanation given the described dual-pipeline setup (C is too narrow), and a memory leak would typically manifest as latency/crash issues, not accuracy degradation (D is false).

mcqs.question: Why does a feature store maintain two physically separate stores (offline and online) rather than one, if the goal is consistency?
options: Because maintaining two stores is required by law for auditability

Because offline and online workloads have very different performance requirements (large historical scans vs single-entity millisecond lookups), so each needs storage optimized for its access pattern — consistency comes from both being fed by the same shared feature definitions, not from using identical storage
Because the online store is only a temporary cache that gets deleted after each request
Because offline and online stores must always contain different feature values by design
mcqs.explanation: The two-store split exists purely for performance fit: the offline store is optimized for scanning large historical volumes (training dataset construction), while the online store is optimized for fast single-entity lookups (serving) — consistency is achieved not by using one physical store, but by having one shared feature computation/definition feed both. There's no legal requirement driving this design (B), the online store is a persistent low-latency store, not a per-request temporary cache (C is false), and both stores should reflect the same underlying feature values, just at different points/granularities in time, not intentionally different values (D is false).

mcqs.question: A churn model is trained using each customer's "total lifetime purchases" feature computed with today's up-to-date total, joined against historical churn labels from six months ago. The model performs excellently offline but poorly in production. What is the likely issue?
options: This is a normal, expected outcome and indicates no problem with the training setup
The model is simply too complex for the dataset size

Future leakage from a violation of point-in-time correctness — the feature reflects purchases the customer hadn't made yet at the historical label's actual timestamp, giving the model information it wouldn't have had at real prediction time
The churn labels themselves must be incorrect
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic point-in-time correctness failure: joining a feature's current value to a historical label lets the model see information from after the label's actual timestamp (later purchases), which it would never have access to at real prediction time — offline metrics look artificially strong because of this leaked future information, then collapse once deployed since production never provides that same illicit information. Model complexity isn't implicated by this specific data-leakage pattern (B), this is a genuine problem, not expected or acceptable behavior (C is false), and the issue described is about feature timing, not label correctness (D is a different, unrelated concern).

mcqs.question: A team silently updates a shared feature's definition (fixing a bug in how a rolling average is computed) without versioning it. What is the risk to already-deployed models using that feature?
options: No risk — bug fixes to feature definitions always improve every model using them automatically
Feature versioning has no relationship to model correctness after deployment
This only matters for models that haven't been deployed yet

Deployed models trained on the old feature definition will now receive inputs computed differently than what they were trained on, an unplanned and undocumented change equivalent to introducing training-serving skew after the fact
mcqs.explanation: Without versioning, an in-place feature definition change silently alters the inputs a live model receives, even though the model was trained on the old definition's behavior — this is functionally the same problem as training-serving skew, just introduced after deployment rather than at launch, which is exactly why feature versioning exists: a deployed model should keep receiving the exact feature version it was trained against until deliberately retrained. Bug fixes don't automatically "improve" a model trained on the old, buggy behavior — the model learned patterns relative to that old computation (A is false), the risk applies specifically to already-deployed models using the feature, not unrelated future ones (C is backwards), and feature versioning is directly tied to maintaining model correctness post-deployment (D is false).

mcqs.question: "Days since last login" is implemented in Python/pandas for training and separately in Java for serving. Both implementations look correct when reviewed independently. What makes this setup risky?
options: Having two independent implementations of the same feature concept, written separately, creates the exact conditions for training-serving skew — subtle edge-case differences (timezone handling, how "never logged in" is treated) can silently diverge without either implementation looking wrong in isolation
This setup is only risky if one of the two languages has a known bug in its standard library
Two implementations are always fine as long as both pass their own unit tests
This pattern is standard best practice and carries no additional risk versus a single shared implementation
mcqs.explanation: The risk isn't about either implementation being individually wrong — it's that two independently maintained implementations of the same feature concept are extremely likely to diverge on some edge case over time, and neither team would necessarily notice, since each implementation can be internally self-consistent and still disagree with the other. Passing unit tests within each implementation doesn't guarantee agreement between them (C is false, since tests are typically written against each implementation's own expected behavior), and dual, independently-written implementations are exactly the anti-pattern feature stores are designed to eliminate, not a best practice (D is false); no specific standard-library bug needs to exist for this risk to materialize (B is too narrow).

mcqs.question: A single small team maintains three models, all reading features from one well-governed, shared SQL table used identically in both training and serving. Do they need a full feature-store platform?
options: Yes, a full platform is mandatory for any production ML system regardless of scale

Not necessarily — a well-governed shared table already solves most of the training-serving skew problem cheaply at this scale; a full platform's added value (point-in-time joins, cross-team governance) becomes worth the overhead mainly as models/teams multiply
No, feature stores are only useful for real-time serving, and this team should never adopt one even at larger scale
Full feature-store platforms provide no benefit over a shared table under any circumstances
mcqs.explanation: This matches the topic's explicit decision guidance: a lightweight, well-governed shared table already captures most of the skew-prevention benefit for a small setup with genuine shared read access, and the extra cost of a full platform (point-in-time join automation, cross-team feature governance) pays off more clearly as the number of models and teams grows. A full platform isn't mandatory at every scale (A overclaims), the team may well benefit from a full platform later as they grow, so "never" is too strong (C is false), and full platforms do provide real added value over shared tables at larger scale, specifically around point-in-time correctness and governance (D is false).
